Paper_name: Prioritised self-referential processing is modulated by emotional arousal
Summary: This study investigates how emotional valence and arousal affect the self-prioritisation effect, where self-related stimuli are processed more efficiently. Experiment 1 used a label-shape matching task across four mood states, finding that higher arousal levels strengthened the self-prioritisation effect, while valence had no reliable impact. Experiment 2 showed that alerting cues, which increase arousal, also enhanced the self-prioritisation effect. Experiment 3 confirmed that alerting cues did not affect reward processing in a similar task, suggesting arousal selectively modulates self-referential processing.
Author: Haoyue Qian, Zhiguo Wang, Chao Li, Xiangping Gao
Conclusion: The main results demonstrate that emotional arousal, but not valence, modulates self-referential processing. Higher arousal levels, induced by mood states or alerting cues, reliably increased the self-prioritisation effect in a label-shape matching task. This modulation appears specific to self-referential processing, as arousal did not affect reward processing in a control experiment.
